Name: LLVM
SDKs & notable repos: Clang, LLD, libc++, MLIR, Polly — one monorepo
Downloadable / offline docs: Docs build from source; released as HTML per version
Notes: The dominant compiler infrastructure. `LangRef.html` is the IR specification and the single most useful document here.

Name: Clang
Notes: The Internals Manual explains how a real industrial frontend is structured.

Name: MLIR
SDKs & notable repos: Dialect infrastructure; used by XLA, TVM, Triton, CIRCT, Flang
Notes: The most important compiler-infrastructure development of the last decade. The Toy tutorial is the way in.

Name: GCC
Downloadable / offline docs: Full manuals as HTML, PDF and info
Notes: The internals manual (`gccint`) is dense but authoritative. Still the reference for many targets LLVM handles less well.

Name: Cranelift
SDKs & notable repos: Fast code generator used by Wasmtime and Rust's debug backend
Notes: Designed for compile speed and verifiability rather than peak output. A useful contrast with LLVM.

Name: QBE
SDKs & notable repos: A compact backend aiming for 70% of LLVM's performance at 10% of the complexity
Notes: Small enough to read entirely. Excellent if LLVM is too large to approach.

Name: chibicc
SDKs & notable repos: A small C compiler developed in readable, incremental commits
Downloadable / offline docs: Read the git history commit by commit
Notes: Rui Ueyama's teaching compiler. The commit sequence *is* the tutorial.

Name: Rust
SDKs & notable repos: Cargo, rustup, clippy, rust-analyzer; MIR and borrow checker in-tree
Downloadable / offline docs: All books ship offline with rustup (`rustup doc`)
Notes: The rustc dev guide is one of the best explanations of a modern compiler's internals ever published openly.

Name: rustc dev guide
SDKs & notable repos: Query-based compilation, HIR, MIR, borrow checking, codegen
Notes: Read this even if you never touch Rust. It explains incremental and query-based compiler architecture better than any textbook.

Name: Go
SDKs & notable repos: Full toolchain in-tree; the compiler is written in Go
Downloadable / offline docs: `go doc` offline; spec is one readable page
Notes: The Go spec is short enough to read in a sitting — a rare virtue. The runtime source (scheduler, GC) is also unusually approachable.

Name: Zig
SDKs & notable repos: Self-hosted compiler; comptime; also works as a C/C++ cross-compiler
Notes: `comptime` is the most interesting language-design idea in recent systems languages.

Name: C++ standardization (WG21)
Notes: Reading WG21 papers is the only way to understand why C++ is shaped as it is. cppreference.com is the practical reference.

Name: C standardization (WG14)
SDKs & notable repos: Working drafts are free; the final standard is not
Notes: The latest working draft is functionally the standard for most purposes.

Name: Swift
SDKs & notable repos: SwiftPM, swift-syntax; SIL is a documented intermediate language
Downloadable / offline docs: Docs site; The Swift Programming Language book free
Notes: SIL (Swift Intermediate Language) is well documented and worth studying as a high-level IR design.

Name: CPython
Downloadable / offline docs: Full docs downloadable as HTML/PDF/EPUB archives
Notes: The developer guide now includes solid internals documentation. `dis` plus `ceval.c` is a practical VM course.

Name: PyPy
Notes: Generating a JIT from an interpreter specification is a genuinely different idea. Read the architecture docs.

Name: OpenJDK
SDKs & notable repos: HotSpot, C1/C2, G1 and ZGC collectors, JVMTI
Downloadable / offline docs: JLS and JVMS free as PDF/HTML
Notes: The JVM Specification is the best-written VM spec in existence. Read it before any JVM internals material.

Name: GraalVM
SDKs & notable repos: Truffle language framework, native image, Graal JIT
Notes: Truffle — building languages as AST interpreters that partial-evaluate into fast code — is the most interesting runtime research shipping in production.

Name: .NET runtime
SDKs & notable repos: RyuJIT, CoreCLR, the BCL; extensive in-repo design docs
Notes: `docs/design/` in dotnet/runtime is a treasure of real runtime engineering writing.

Name: Roslyn
SDKs & notable repos: Compiler-as-a-service: syntax trees, semantic model, analyzers
Notes: The clearest production example of an IDE-oriented incremental compiler.

Name: V8
SDKs & notable repos: Ignition interpreter, TurboFan and Maglev JITs, Orinoco GC
Notes: The V8 blog posts on hidden classes and inline caches are the standard explanation of dynamic-language optimization.

Name: Node.js
Downloadable / offline docs: Docs downloadable as JSON/HTML per version

Name: LuaJIT
Notes: Mike Pall's tracing JIT remains among the most impressive single-author compiler engineering efforts anywhere.

Name: Lua
SDKs & notable repos: The whole language in a ~25,000-line C codebase
Notes: One of the most readable language implementations in existence. A good first real interpreter to study.

Name: GHC (Haskell)
SDKs & notable repos: Core, STG and Cmm intermediate languages, all documented
Notes: The Core-to-STG-to-Cmm pipeline is the reference for compiling lazy functional languages.

Name: OCaml
SDKs & notable repos: Dune, opam; the compiler is small and readable
Notes: Frequently the implementation language of choice for compiler research, for good reasons.

Name: Erlang/OTP
Notes: BEAM's scheduler and process isolation design is unlike anything else in this list.

Name: WebAssembly spec
SDKs & notable repos: Formal semantics, with a reference interpreter in OCaml
Notes: A fully formally specified mainstream VM — rare, and worth reading as an example of how to specify one.

Name: Wasmtime
Notes: The reference standalone runtime.

Name: ECMAScript specification
Notes: Surprisingly readable once you learn the abstract-operation notation.

Name: TC39 proposals
SDKs & notable repos: Every JS language proposal by stage
Notes: Watch the language evolve in public.

Name: Java Language & VM Specifications
Notes: The JVMS is a model of how to specify a virtual machine.

Name: tree-sitter
SDKs & notable repos: Incremental GLR parsing; grammars for 100+ languages; bindings everywhere
Notes: Now the standard parsing layer for editors. The incremental re-parsing design is the interesting part.

Name: ANTLR
SDKs & notable repos: ALL(*) parsing; targets Java, C#, Python, Go, C++, JS
Notes: The practical choice when you need a parser for a real grammar quickly.

Name: GNU Bison
Downloadable / offline docs: Manual as HTML, PDF and info; releases at https://ftp.gnu.org/gnu/bison/
Notes: Still worth learning for the grammar theory, even if you ship tree-sitter. www.gnu.org blocks our verification network at the host level — the project is live (ftp.gnu.org and savannah both responded 200) and the manual loads normally in a browser.

Name: LLVM Kaleidoscope tutorial
SDKs & notable repos: Build a working language with an LLVM backend, chapter by chapter
Notes: The canonical 'my first LLVM frontend' path.

Name: Compiler Explorer (godbolt)
SDKs & notable repos: Live compilation to assembly across dozens of compilers and languages; self-hostable
Downloadable / offline docs: Whole site runs locally from the repo
Notes: The single most useful interactive tool in this field. Also shows LLVM IR, MIR and GIMPLE, not just assembly.

Name: cppreference
SDKs & notable repos: The practical C and C++ reference, tracking the standard closely
Downloadable / offline docs: Full offline archive available for download
Notes: 403s to bots, fine in a browser. More usable than the standard itself for day-to-day work.

Name: Rustonomicon
SDKs & notable repos: Unsafe Rust, aliasing rules, variance, drop order
Notes: The place where Rust’s memory model is actually explained.

Name: Racket
SDKs & notable repos: Language-oriented programming; `#lang` lets you define whole new languages
Downloadable / offline docs: Full docs ship with the installation
Notes: Built specifically for making languages. If you want to prototype a language design quickly, start here.

Name: R7RS Scheme
Notes: A complete language specification you can read in an evening. Excellent calibration for what a spec can be.

Name: SICP
SDKs & notable repos: Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs, including the metacircular evaluator
Downloadable / offline docs: Free PDF; a cleaner HTML edition at https://sarabander.github.io/sicp/
Notes: Chapters 4 and 5 — building an evaluator and a register machine — are the relevant part for this topic.

Name: Essentials of Compilation
SDKs & notable repos: Jeremy Siek’s incremental compiler course book, in Racket and Python editions
Notes: Builds a compiler in small verified increments. A strong complement to Crafting Interpreters.

Name: Lean 4
SDKs & notable repos: Dependently typed language and proof assistant; also a serious general-purpose language
Downloadable / offline docs: Functional Programming in Lean and Theorem Proving in Lean, both free
Notes: Lean is written largely in Lean, so the compiler source doubles as an advanced example.

Name: Rocq (formerly Coq)
SDKs & notable repos: The proof assistant behind CompCert and Software Foundations
Notes: Renamed from Coq in 2025. Older material still says Coq; it is the same system.

Name: Agda
SDKs & notable repos: Dependently typed functional language and proof assistant

Name: Dafny
SDKs & notable repos: Verification-aware language with an SMT backend
Notes: The most approachable entry into program verification — write preconditions and let Z3 do the work.

Name: matklad’s blog
SDKs & notable repos: Aleksey Kladov on parsers, IDEs, build systems and rust-analyzer internals
Notes: The Pratt parsing article and the IDE-architecture posts are essential reading for anyone building language tooling.

Name: arXiv
SDKs & notable repos: Preprints across all of CS; most systems, ML and PL work appears here before publication
Downloadable / offline docs: Every paper is a free PDF. Bulk access documented at https://info.arxiv.org/help/bulk_data/index.html; a full-text API at export.arxiv.org
Notes: Not peer-reviewed. Treat an arXiv-only paper as a claim, not a result — but it is where you will read almost everything first.

Name: ar5iv
SDKs & notable repos: Renders any arXiv paper as responsive HTML instead of PDF
Notes: Makes papers readable on a phone and searchable in-page. Underused.

Name: alphaXiv
SDKs & notable repos: arXiv papers with a public comment and discussion layer
Notes: Useful when a paper is contested — the discussion often contains the critique you were looking for.

Name: Semantic Scholar
SDKs & notable repos: 200M+ papers with citation graph, influential-citation scoring and TLDR summaries
Downloadable / offline docs: Free Graph API (https://www.semanticscholar.org/product/api), bulk datasets available on request
Notes: The best free citation graph. 'Highly influential citations' is a genuinely useful filter for finding what actually mattered.

Name: OpenAlex
SDKs & notable repos: Fully open catalogue of works, authors, venues and institutions; successor to Microsoft Academic Graph
Downloadable / offline docs: Entirely free API with no key required; complete database snapshots downloadable
Notes: The only large-scale bibliographic database that is open all the way down, including bulk snapshots.

Name: DBLP
SDKs & notable repos: Authoritative CS bibliography — complete author and venue listings
Notes: The fastest way to find everything a given researcher has published, and to see a conference's full programme by year.

Name: OpenReview
SDKs & notable repos: ICLR, NeurIPS, COLM and dozens of other venues — papers plus the full review threads
Notes: Reading the reviews and author rebuttals teaches you how the field evaluates work. Nothing else exposes this.

Name: CORE
SDKs & notable repos: Aggregates 300M+ open-access papers from repositories worldwide
Notes: Good for finding the green open-access copy when a publisher's version is paywalled.

Name: Unpaywall
SDKs & notable repos: Finds legal free copies of paywalled papers via DOI
Notes: Legal, author-deposited copies only. Install the extension and most paywalls simply stop appearing.

Name: Papers We Love
SDKs & notable repos: A curated, categorised repository of classic CS papers with local meetup talks
Downloadable / offline docs: Repo cloneable; many PDFs mirrored in-repo
Notes: The best starting point if you do not yet know which papers matter in a subfield.

Name: The Morning Paper (archive)
Notes: No longer updated, but the back catalogue of ~1000 summarised papers is one of the great free CS resources.

Name: USENIX Proceedings
SDKs & notable repos: OSDI, SOSP (co-published), NSDI, ATC, FAST, Security — the core systems venues
Downloadable / offline docs: Every paper free, immediately, with no membership. Often with recorded talks
Notes: USENIX made everything open access years before the rest of the field. If a systems paper exists, check here first.

Name: ACM Digital Library
SDKs & notable repos: SIGMOD, ASPLOS, PLDI, POPL, SoCC and the ACM journals
Downloadable / offline docs: Partly open: ACM Open and author-paid OA papers are free; others are paywalled
Notes: 403s to automated clients; loads in a browser. For paywalled items, check arXiv, the author's homepage or Unpaywall first — the free copy usually exists.

Name: IEEE Xplore
SDKs & notable repos: ISCA, MICRO, HPCA and the IEEE journals
Notes: Almost always worth searching the author's page or arXiv instead. Architecture authors in particular post preprints widely.

Name: DROPS / LIPIcs (Dagstuhl)
SDKs & notable repos: ECOOP, ITP, CONCUR, SAT and many theory venues
Downloadable / offline docs: 100% open access, free PDFs, Creative Commons licensed
Notes: A fully open publisher. Every paper, always free, no exceptions.

Name: arXiv cs.PL (Programming Languages)
Notes: See also https://arxiv.org/list/cs.SE/recent for software engineering.

Name: SIGPLAN OpenTOC
SDKs & notable repos: Free, sanctioned access to the tables of contents and papers of PLDI, POPL, ICFP, OOPSLA and SPLASH
Notes: The official free route into SIGPLAN proceedings. Most people do not know this exists and pay or give up instead.

Name: ACM SIGPLAN
SDKs & notable repos: The PL special interest group; PACMPL is its open-access journal
Notes: Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages is gold open access — POPL, PLDI, ICFP and OOPSLA papers are free.

Name: PLDI
SDKs & notable repos: Programming Language Design and Implementation — the compiler-heavy venue
Notes: If you care about compilers rather than type theory, start here.

Name: POPL
SDKs & notable repos: Principles of Programming Languages — the theory venue

Name: SPLASH / OOPSLA
SDKs & notable repos: Object-oriented, applied and practice-oriented PL research

Name: ECOOP
Notes: Published through Dagstuhl, so every paper is free and Creative Commons licensed.

Name: The Art, Science, and Engineering of Programming
SDKs & notable repos: Open-access PL journal with an unusually broad remit
Notes: Publishes work that does not fit the conference mould, including essays and artifacts.

Name: conf.researchr.org
SDKs & notable repos: The hosting platform for most PL and SE conferences — programmes, artifacts, recorded talks
Notes: Browse any recent conference programme here; artifact links are often more useful than the papers.

Name: DROPS / LIPIcs
SDKs & notable repos: ECOOP, ITP, CONCUR, FSCD and other formal-methods venues

Name: LLVM Weekly
Notes: The best way to track what is actually changing in the dominant compiler infrastructure.

Name: Crafting Interpreters
Notes: Build two complete interpreters — a tree-walker in Java and a bytecode VM in C — with every line of code in the text. Free online, beautifully written. The best introduction to this field by a wide margin.

Name: Crafting Interpreters source
Notes: Reference implementations of both interpreters.

Name: Writing a C Compiler
Notes: Nora Sandler's incremental C compiler book; the free blog series it grew from is also still online.

Name: Write a Compiler (blog series)
Notes: The free predecessor to the book. A complete staged project.

Name: chibicc
SDKs & notable repos: Small implementations to read end to end
Notes: A C compiler built in readable incremental commits. Walk the git history as a tutorial.

Name: Lua source
SDKs & notable repos: Small implementations to read end to end
Notes: A complete, fast, widely deployed language in ~25k lines of exceptionally clean C.

Name: QBE
SDKs & notable repos: Small implementations to read end to end
Notes: A compiler backend small enough to actually read, aiming at most of LLVM's performance with a fraction of the complexity.

Name: Let's Build a Compiler (Crenshaw)
SDKs & notable repos: Small implementations to read end to end
Notes: Dated in its target, timeless in its method. Still one of the gentlest introductions.

Name: Stanford CS143 Compilers
Notes: Lexing through code generation, with public assignments building a full COOL compiler.

Name: LLVM Kaleidoscope tutorial
Notes: Get a real language running on a real backend in a weekend.

Name: MLIR Toy tutorial
Notes: The seven-chapter Toy tutorial is the standard entry point to MLIR.

Name: The Go specification
Notes: Short enough to read in one sitting. A model of specification economy.

Name: ECMAScript specification
Notes: Learn to read the abstract-operation notation; it makes JavaScript's oddities explicable.

Name: Java Virtual Machine Specification
Notes: The clearest specification of a virtual machine anywhere. Free.

Name: WebAssembly core spec
Notes: A formally specified VM with a reference interpreter you can read.

Name: tree-sitter
Notes: Write a grammar and get incremental parsing plus editor integration for free.

Name: ANTLR
Notes: When you need a working parser fast.

Name: GNU Bison
Notes: Learn LALR parsing properly once.

Name: LLVM LangRef
Notes: Learn to read LLVM IR. It is a lingua franca across the whole field.

Name: Papers We Love
Notes: Start here when you do not yet know which papers matter. Curated by subfield, with recorded talks.

Name: The Morning Paper archive
Notes: Around a thousand papers summarised in plain language. No longer updated; still one of the best free CS resources.

Name: Semantic Scholar
Notes: Free citation graph. The 'highly influential citations' filter is the fastest way to find what a paper actually changed.

Name: Unpaywall
Notes: Install the extension. Most paywalls stop appearing, legally, because the author deposited a copy.

Name: ar5iv
Notes: Read any arXiv paper as HTML instead of a two-column PDF. Swap arxiv.org/abs for ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html.

Name: rustc dev guide
Notes: Query-based incremental compilation, MIR, borrow checking — explained unusually well. Read it regardless of your language.

Name: Clang Internals Manual
Notes: How an industrial C/C++ frontend is actually organised.

Name: LLVM documentation
Notes: Pass infrastructure, the pass manager, and writing your own passes.

Name: GCC internals (gccint)
Notes: GIMPLE and RTL. Dense, but the only authoritative source.

Name: Roslyn
Notes: Incremental, IDE-first compiler design — a different set of constraints from batch compilation.

Name: Cranelift
Notes: A backend optimized for compile speed and verifiability instead of peak output.

Name: MLIR docs
Notes: Dialects, regions, the pattern rewriting infrastructure.

Name: MLIR
Notes: Start with the Toy tutorial, then read a real dialect.

Name: LLVM monorepo
Notes: MLIR lives here alongside LLVM proper; read them together.

Name: Apache TVM
Notes: Domain-specific compilation with autotuning.

Name: OpenXLA
Notes: A production ML compiler with genuinely good internal documentation.

Name: V8 docs and blog
Notes: Hidden classes, inline caches, and the tiering between Ignition, Maglev and TurboFan.

Name: V8 source
Notes: Large but navigable if you enter through a blog post's named files.

Name: OpenJDK
Notes: HotSpot's C2, plus G1 and ZGC — the most mature GC implementations available to read.

Name: JVM Specification
Notes: Read the spec before the implementation.

Name: GraalVM
Notes: Truffle and partial evaluation: build an AST interpreter, get a JIT. A genuinely different approach.

Name: .NET runtime design docs
Notes: `docs/design/` contains real engineering writing on RyuJIT and the GC.

Name: PyPy
Notes: Meta-tracing — generating a JIT from an interpreter definition.

Name: LuaJIT
Notes: Trace compilation at its most refined.

Name: CPython developer guide
Notes: The bytecode VM, the specializing adaptive interpreter, and the C API.

Name: Types and Programming Languages (TAPL)
Notes: The standard text. Companion OCaml implementations are free from this page.

Name: Software Foundations
Notes: Machine-checked PL theory in Coq. Free, enormous, and rigorous.

Name: PLAI — Programming Languages: Application and Interpretation
Notes: Free book building language features by implementing them.

Name: GHC user guide
Notes: Where advanced type-system features actually ship. The extensions documentation is a tour of modern type theory.

Name: OCaml
Notes: The practical implementation language of PL research.

Name: WebAssembly core specification
Notes: Formal semantics with a reference interpreter.

Name: Wasmtime
Notes: The reference runtime; read it with Cranelift.

Name: Wasmer
Notes: Alternative backends and a different design philosophy.

Name: WAMR
Notes: Wasm on microcontrollers.

Name: Cornell CS6120 — Advanced Compilers
Notes: Adrian Sampson's self-guided PhD course. All materials, readings and a working IR are public. Outstanding.

Name: SIGPLAN
Notes: The umbrella for PL conferences, with open-access policies.

Name: PLDI
Notes: Implementation-focused.

Name: POPL
Notes: Theory-focused.

Name: WG21 papers
Notes: Language design argued in public, at length.

Name: TC39 proposals
Notes: The same, for JavaScript, and easier to follow.

Name: Tsoding Daily
Notes: Livestreamed low-level building: compilers, interpreters, OS-ish projects in C and Zig.

Name: CppCon
Notes: The C++ conference — where the memory-model and atomics talks live.

Name: Strange Loop Conference
Notes: The Strange Loop channel: distributed systems, databases and language talks from the conference.

Name: Computerphile
Notes: Short, well-made explainers; the right first stop before a spec.

Name: Neso Academy
Notes: Unit-by-unit university course playlists (OS, compiler design); verify against OSTEP and the dragon book.

Name: USENIX
Notes: Conference recordings for most USENIX papers — free video, the fastest route into a systems paper.

Name: InfoQ
Notes: Conference keynotes and architecture talks — good for orientation, verify specifics elsewhere.

Name: Papers We Love
Notes: Recorded paper walkthroughs — watch one before you read the PDF.

Name: PyCon US
Notes: The full PyCon archive: CPython internals, JIT work, type systems, packaging.

Name: C++Now
Notes: The Boost-flavoured C++ conference; more language-design and metaprogramming than CppCon.

Name: Meeting C++
Notes: European C++ conference recordings, including standardisation talks.

Name: Stanford CS143 — Compilers (Alex Aiken)
Notes: Short, tightly cut lectures: lexing through code generation and register allocation.

Name: LLVM Developers' Meetings
Notes: Slides and recordings for every LLVM dev meeting going back years — the single best compiler-implementation archive.

Name: PyCon US
Notes: Full talk archive on the site and on the PyCon US channel; interpreter internals talks every year.

Name: Strange Loop
Notes: Language-design and implementation talks, free.

Name: FOSDEM video archive
Notes: Programming-language and compiler devrooms.

Name: No official channel for PLDI, POPL or ICFP
Notes: Checked on 2026-10-09. Papers live in the ACM DL and PACMPL (open); talks surface on author pages and at Strange Loop.
